newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi water use drops after halt to grain exports.
newsitem.headline: Saudi water use drops after halt to grain exports.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's year-old decision to stop grain exports has drastically cut water use in the desert kingdom, its agriculture and water minister said in remarks published on Tuesday.

Abdullah bin Abdul-Aziz bin Muammar told the Arabic-language business daily al-Eqtisadiah that the kingdom would grow wheat and barley only to meet local demand and boost the country's strategic reserves, but not for export.
The decision to stop exports of the subsidised commodities had boosted water reserves.

Water consumption by wheat farmers dropped to 1,850 million cubic metres in 1996 from 6,990 million in 1992, while water used by barley growers fell to 510 million cubic metres from 2,010 million in the same period.
Muammar said last month the kingdom had cut wheat and barley production to a total of 1.7 million tonnes in 1996 from six million in 1992.
Analysts estimate Saudi Arabia produced some 1.2 million tonnes of wheat and around 450,000 tonnes of barley last year. Local wheat consumption is about 1.8 million tonnes.
They forecast barley imports by the world's single largest barley buyer of around six million tonnes this year.

Muammar told al-Eqtisadiah his ministry had taken a number of measures to conserve underground water, including halting the execution of proposed animal feed projects and transforming them to other farming schemes that rely on less water.
It also banned drilling of wells in 50 sites and stopped the distribution of agricultural plots in these areas.

The daily said the Saudi government was also considering measures to force every farmer to install water meters on existing artesian wells to rationalise water use. It might also remove aid from farmers who violated the rules.
